reason: Wording: checked twice against transcriptions of the 1895 Atlanta Offering, not against a quotation site. The Lehigh African American Poetry digital anthology transcription of Atlanta Offering: Poems (1895) gives the final stanza as Music to soothe all its sorrow, / Till war and crime shall cease; / And the hearts of men grown tender / Girdle the world with peace. That is the shipped wording to the letter, including the comma after sorrow, the semicolon after cease, and the absence of a comma after tender. Lineation is four lines with the capitals Music, Till, And, Girdle at the line heads, as required, and the stanza closes on a full stop. Attribution: Harper's own poem, not on the misattribution list, no speaker question since it is the poet in her own voice. Scope: 1895, poetry, not scripture, not a lyric (it is a poem about making songs, which is a different thing), nothing needing a warning. Tag: Poetry, the form of the work. Cap: shipped.js gives frances ellen watkins harper at 0 of 3, not banned, nothing shipped, no near opening, and she appears once in the month's poetry-drama proposals, so the one-per-month rule holds. Source line: 137 characters, leads with the name, no dash. Theme: hearts grown tender girdling the world with peace is squarely Justice and Service, and it is warm rather than bleak at six in the morning. ONE ERROR FOUND, and it is in the evidence, not on the card. The evidence locator calls this the eighth and final stanza. The poem has SEVEN stanzas: Let me make the songs for the people; Not for the clashing of sabres; Let me make the songs for the weary; Let me sing for little children; I would sing for the poor and aged; Our world, so worn and weary; and then this one. Both the Academy of American Poets text and the Lehigh transcription count seven. The shipped source line says only the closing stanza, which is correct, so the line ships unharmed; but the evidence field must be corrected to the seventh and final stanza before it travels, or a later hand will read eighth off the evidence and print a stanza number that does not exist. Two smaller points that do not refute: the source's Poems (George S. Ferguson, 1896) follows the poets.org credit, and the wording was in fact read in the 1895 Atlanta Offering, which the source honestly names as the first printing; and Lehigh also holds a Poems dated 1895, so the 1896 date is a publisher's printing year taken from a standard reference rather than from a scan, which the source's semicolon construction already concedes.
